title: A Ruler from Little Bethlehem
overview: In a time of siege and humiliation, Micah promises a coming ruler from David's small hometown who will bring peace and security, and a future where God strips away the weapons and idols the people had trusted.

parts.label: Jerusalem under siege (v. 1)
parts.note: The city is surrounded, and its leader is struck on the cheek, a deep public insult. Scholars are unsure whether this pictures the Assyrian siege of Micah's day or the later Babylonian one.

parts.label: A ruler from Bethlehem (v. 2)
parts.note: Bethlehem was the small hometown of King David, so this promises a new king from David's family, whose roots go back a very long way. Christians read this as pointing to Jesus, born in Bethlehem, and the Gospel of Matthew quotes this verse.

parts.label: Waiting, then a shepherd (vv. 3-4)
parts.note: The people will suffer until a woman gives birth; she may be the ruler's mother or Israel pictured as a woman in labor, and scholars are unsure which. Then the scattered will come home, and this ruler will care for them like a shepherd, backed by the LORD's own strength.

parts.label: Peace against Assyria (vv. 5-6)
parts.note: Assyria was the great empire threatening Judah at the time, and the promise is that this ruler will be the people's peace. Naming seven leaders and then eight is a Hebrew way of saying more than enough, and they will turn the tables by invading Assyria, here called the land of Nimrod after a legendary founder of its cities.

parts.label: Like dew, like a lion (vv. 7-9)
parts.note: The surviving few of Israel are pictured among the nations as dew, a gift that arrives without any human help, and as a lion tearing through sheep with no one able to rescue them. The second image is plainly violent, describing triumph over enemies, and how the two pictures relate is debated.

parts.label: God removes false supports (vv. 10-15)
parts.note: God says he will take away what the people relied on instead of him: war horses, chariots, fortified cities, spells, carved idols, sacred standing stones and Asherah poles, wooden poles linked to the worship of a goddess. The chapter ends with God's anger turned on the nations that refused to listen.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether verse 2 originally spoke of a coming king from David's line that later found its fullest meaning in Jesus, or was a direct prediction of Jesus from the start, including whether the ruler's ancient origins mean David's old family line or an existence before time began.
think: What do people tend to rely on to feel safe, and what happens to them when those things are taken away?
